parsed.business_context: SMM (Social Media Marketing) reseller panel. ~44k users, ~967k orders. Multi-PSP balance top-up (Cryptomus, Coinbase, Payeer, Perfect Money, manual USDT/BTC). Operator reports active account-takeover incidents. Revenue-critical: every lost balance or processor compromise directly damages operator monetization.

assets.name: User Account Balances
assets.rationale: Direct theft vector. Attackers monetize by withdrawing user funds. Operator liable for refunds. Drives revenue loss and platform credibility collapse.

assets.name: Payment Processor API Keys (Cryptomus, Coinbase, Payeer, Perfect Money)
assets.rationale: Compromised keys grant direct withdrawal access to operator's merchant accounts and customer deposits. Single point of failure for all payment flows. Attacker can drain operator reserves.

assets.name: Admin Panel Access
assets.rationale: Full site control: user management, payment settings, balance manipulation, log deletion. Enables cover-up of previous breaches and wholesale account takeovers.

assets.name: User Credentials (Username + Password Hash)
assets.rationale: Enables account takeover when combined with weak hashing or rainbow tables. Attacker can mass-breach accounts and drain balances. Also resale value on dark market.

assets.name: Session Tokens / Auth Cookies
assets.rationale: Hijacking via XSS or theft grants account access without password. Enables CSRF on balance-changing actions. High velocity attack surface.

assets.name: Upstream Service Credentials (SMM API keys, resale APIs)
assets.rationale: Compromised keys allow attacker to place fraudulent orders and credit own balance without paying. Enables service abuse and financial loss via refund cycles.

assets.name: Transaction and Audit Logs
assets.rationale: Attackers delete/modify logs to cover traces of balance theft or ATO. Loss of audit trail hampers incident investigation and regulatory compliance (GDPR/PCI).

assets.name: User Target / Resale Data (social accounts, service types, volumes)
assets.rationale: Competitors and affiliated criminals value customer lists and order patterns. Lower immediate financial impact than balance theft, but enables secondary monetization.

actors.name: Financially-Motivated Criminal (Opportunistic/Volume)
actors.goal: Maximize short-term monetary gain: steal balances, resell credentials, abuse refund loops.
actors.notes: Primary realistic threat. Uses public tools (burp, Shodan, public exploits). Targets weak auth, IDOR, unsigned webhooks. Fast and noisy; will abandon if friction rises. Volume-based attacks (credential stuffing, brute force).

actors.name: Automated Botnet / Scanner (Script-Driven)
actors.goal: Discover and exploit easy wins: default credentials, unpatched vulns, weak endpoints.
actors.notes: Drives mass ATO via password spraying. No persistence; exploits and moves on. High noise. Triggered by published CVEs affecting PHP/Smarty/Perfect Panel forks.

actors.name: Competitor (Motivated, Stealthy)
actors.goal: Steal customer lists, disrupt service, poach users, damage reputation.
actors.notes: Targets user data exfiltration and prolonged service unavailability. More patient and stealthy than criminals. Willing to pivot through codebase for advantage. Targets confidentiality over immediate theft.

actors.name: Malicious Admin / Insider
actors.goal: Steal payment keys, exfiltrate user data, sabotage operations.
actors.notes: Already has access; can bypass most controls. Can modify logs. Enables cover-up of other breaches. Lower probability but catastrophic impact. Out-of-model for penetration testing (test assumes legitimate admin honesty).

trust_boundaries.name: Anonymous User → Web App Login
trust_boundaries.auth_check: Credential verification against user table; rate limit on failed attempts
trust_boundaries.failure_mode: No rate limit enables brute force; weak password rules; SQL injection in login query; unsalted password hash

trust_boundaries.name: Authenticated User → Web App (General User Actions)
trust_boundaries.data_crossing: Session token in cookie/header; order requests (amount, service type); balance queries; profile updates
trust_boundaries.auth_check: Session token validation; ownership check on resource IDs (IDOR on orders, balance)
trust_boundaries.failure_mode: Missing IDOR checks; session fixation; CSRF on balance-changing actions; no server-side validation of price/balance fields; race condition on concurrent balance deduction

trust_boundaries.name: User-A Data ↔ User-B Data (Tenant Isolation)
trust_boundaries.data_crossing: User balance, order history, refund status, personal info, targets/leads
trust_boundaries.auth_check: Ownership verification on /api/order/ID, /api/balance, /api/user/ID; authorization query in DB WHERE user_id = current_user_id
trust_boundaries.failure_mode: Sequential/guessable user/order IDs; missing WHERE clause in query; user can modify ID in request to access other users' data; refund endpoint has no authorization check

trust_boundaries.name: User / Authenticated Admin → Admin Panel
trust_boundaries.data_crossing: Admin settings (PSP keys), user ledger, configuration, logs, payment processor webhooks
trust_boundaries.auth_check: Role-based access control (is_admin flag); admin-only middleware on /admin/*; admin user authentication
trust_boundaries.failure_mode: is_admin flag stored client-side (cookie, session, local storage) without server validation; SQL injection on admin login; privilege escalation via parameter tampering (?role=admin); default admin credentials; no MFA

trust_boundaries.name: Web App → Payment Processors (Cryptomus, Coinbase, Payeer, Perfect Money) Webhooks
trust_boundaries.data_crossing: Webhook callback with payment status (success/failure), amount, user ID, transaction hash; balance credit/debit instruction
trust_boundaries.auth_check: HMAC signature verification on webhook payload; IP whitelist of processor servers (if applicable)
trust_boundaries.failure_mode: Unsigned webhooks; weak HMAC algorithm (predictable key, length-extension vulnerable); no state/nonce check; timing attack on signature verification; webhook reflected back without idempotency check (double-credit)

trust_boundaries.name: Web App → Payment Processors (API Requests)
trust_boundaries.data_crossing: API key in Authorization header; balance queries, withdrawal requests, transaction status queries
trust_boundaries.auth_check: Bearer token in header; HTTPS encryption in transit
trust_boundaries.failure_mode: API keys logged in plaintext in error messages; keys stored unencrypted in DB or config; keys exposed in source code; MITM if HTTPS not enforced; no request signing (attacker can replay requests)

trust_boundaries.name: Web App → Database (MySQL/PostgreSQL)
trust_boundaries.data_crossing: User credentials, balances, orders, payment processor settings, logs, admin actions
trust_boundaries.auth_check: Parameterized queries; least-privilege DB user (read/write, no DROP/CREATE); network isolation
trust_boundaries.failure_mode: SQL injection in any query; unsanitized user input in WHERE clauses; string concatenation instead of prepared statements; weak DB password; DB exposed to internet; plaintext password storage (no bcrypt/Argon2)

trust_boundaries.name: Browser → Web App (Client-Side Rendering)
trust_boundaries.data_crossing: Session cookie, DOM with balance/user data, local storage with tokens, form inputs
trust_boundaries.auth_check: CSP (Content Security Policy); SameSite=Strict on cookies; Secure flag on cookies (HTTPS-only); anti-CSRF tokens on state-changing actions
trust_boundaries.failure_mode: Stored/reflected/DOM XSS enables session theft; balance rendered in HTML (attacker modifies DOM); CSRF on refund/order endpoints (no CSRF token); session token in localStorage (XSS steals it); unsanitized user input in Smarty templates

trust_boundaries.name: Web App → File System (Upload / Inclusion)
trust_boundaries.data_crossing: User-uploaded files (avatars, documents); application config files; logs
trust_boundaries.auth_check: File type validation (whitelist, magic bytes); path traversal checks; executable bit not set on uploads
trust_boundaries.failure_mode: Arbitrary file upload (PHP shell); path traversal in upload (/../../config.php); LFI via ?page=../../config.php; backup files readable (.bak, ~, .git); no extension check (upload .php5 as jpg)

stride_threats.threat: Credential stuffing / brute force on /login endpoint with no rate limit, enabling account takeover of high-value users.
SQL injection in login query (username' OR '1'='1--) bypasses credential check.
User password stored as plaintext or unsalted MD5 hash; rainbow table enables offline cracking if DB breached.
Resource exhaustion on login endpoint (no rate limit); attacker locks out legitimate users via repeated failed attempts.

stride_threats.boundary: Authenticated User → Web App (General User Actions)
stride_threats.threat: Session hijacking via stored XSS in username or profile field; attacker steals cookie and impersonates user.

stride_threats.boundary: Authenticated User → Web App (General User Actions)
stride_threats.threat: CSRF on balance-affecting endpoints (place order, refund); attacker tricks user into authorizing unwanted action.

stride_threats.boundary: Authenticated User → Web App (General User Actions)
stride_threats.threat: Client-trusted price/balance field in order request; attacker modifies amount before submit (e.g., order price = 0).

stride_threats.boundary: Authenticated User → Web App (General User Actions)
stride_threats.threat: Race condition on balance check and deduction; concurrent requests both pass check and both deduct, allowing overdraft.

stride_threats.boundary: Authenticated User → Web App (General User Actions)
stride_threats.threat: User creates mass orders to exhaust own balance as griefing; operator absorbs service cost.
IDOR on order endpoint: /api/order/123 returns order details even if user does not own order 123; attacker reads all orders.
IDOR on refund endpoint: /api/refund/ORDER_ID has no authorization check; attacker refunds orders belonging to other users.
IDOR on balance endpoint: /api/balance/USER_ID returns balance for any user ID; attacker enumerates all user balances.
Privilege escalation via parameter tampering: POST /api/user-role?role=admin or is_admin=1 in session cookie.
Brute force admin password on /admin/login with no rate limit (same vulns as user login, but targets single admin user).
SQL injection on admin login bypasses authentication and returns admin user without password check.
Default admin credentials not changed (admin/admin, admin/password); attacker logs in directly.

stride_threats.boundary: Web App → Payment Processors (Cryptomus, Coinbase, Payeer, Perfect Money) Webhooks
stride_threats.threat: Unsigned webhook endpoint: attacker forges balance-credit webhook (POST /webhook/balance-top-up with amount=$100000) without HMAC signature.

stride_threats.boundary: Web App → Payment Processors (Cryptomus, Coinbase, Payeer, Perfect Money) Webhooks
stride_threats.threat: Webhook signature uses weak HMAC algorithm (e.g., HMAC-MD5, predictable key); attacker forges valid signature.

stride_threats.boundary: Web App → Payment Processors (Cryptomus, Coinbase, Payeer, Perfect Money) Webhooks
stride_threats.threat: Webhook idempotency not enforced: attacker replays same webhook multiple times; balance credited multiple times for one transaction.

stride_threats.boundary: Web App → Payment Processors (Cryptomus, Coinbase, Payeer, Perfect Money) Webhooks
stride_threats.threat: Webhook processing runs with elevated privilege; attacker credits any user via webhook tampering.
API keys logged in error messages or debug output; attacker reads error page and steals key.
API keys stored plaintext in database or config.php; SQL injection or file read exposes keys.
SQL injection in user search or filter endpoint; attacker modifies balance directly (UPDATE users SET balance=9999999 WHERE id=123).
SQL injection enables data exfiltration: attacker queries user table and dumps all credentials and balances.
SQL injection with DROP/DELETE: attacker deletes entire order history or user table.
Stored XSS in support ticket subject line; when admin views ticket, JavaScript steals admin session cookie.
Reflected XSS in order details page (/?order_id=<script>alert(1)</script>); attacker sends link to user, steals session.
DOM-based XSS: client-side JS processes user input unsafely and injects into innerHTML.
CSRF on refund endpoint; attacker embeds on external site and tricks user into visiting.
Arbitrary file upload: attacker uploads PHP shell as avatar.jpg.php or avatar.phtml; executes via HTTP request.
Path traversal on file read (LFI): /download?file=../../config.php exposes config with payment keys.
Backup files readable in web root (.bak, .git, config.php~, .env.bak) contain credentials and API keys.

children.label: 1. Steal User Account Balances (Direct Monetization)
1.1. Mass Account Takeover via Credential Brute Force
1.1.1. No rate limit on /login endpoint
1.1.2. Attacker sprays common passwords (password123, 123456) against user list
1.1.3. Weak password policy (no minimum length, no complexity)
1.2. Session Hijacking via Stored XSS
1.2.1. Stored XSS in username / profile display field
1.2.2. Stored XSS in support ticket subject / message
1.2.3. Attacker crafts payload that steals session cookie on page load
1.2.4. No Content Security Policy (CSP) to block script execution
1.3. IDOR on Balance Endpoint
1.3.1. GET /api/balance/USER_ID lacks authorization check (no WHERE user_id = current_user)
1.3.2. User IDs are sequential (1, 2, 3, ...) enabling enumeration
1.3.3. Attacker reads all user balances, identifies high-value targets
1.4. Refund Without Authorization (IDOR on Refund Endpoint)
1.4.1. POST /api/refund/ORDER_ID has no authorization check
1.4.2. Attacker refunds orders belonging to other users to their own account
1.4.3. No per-user refund limit or refund eligibility window check
1.5. Race Condition on Balance Deduction
1.5.1. No atomic transaction on balance check + deduction
1.5.2. Attacker sends concurrent order requests before balance is deducted
1.5.3. Both requests pass balance check, both deduct; user goes negative
1.6. Client-Trusted Price/Balance Field
1.6.1. Order request includes price field controlled by client
1.6.2. Attacker sets price=0 to get service for free
1.6.3. No server-side price validation against catalog
1.7. Webhook Spoofing: Forge Balance Credit
1.7.1. Webhook endpoint has no HMAC signature verification
1.7.2. Attacker crafts POST /webhook/balance-credit with user_id and amount
1.7.3. Endpoint credits balance without verifying webhook origin
1.8. Coupon / Voucher Abuse
1.8.1. Coupon code has no per-user limit; can be reused indefinitely
1.8.2. Coupon codes are guessable (WELCOME, NEWYEAR2025, TEST)
1.8.3. Stack multiple coupons to 100%+ off via arithmetic overflow
1.8.4. No cap on total discount per order
2. Compromise Payment Processor API Keys (Operator Fund Drain)
2.1. Exfiltrate Keys from Database
2.1.1. Keys stored plaintext in users/settings table
2.1.2. SQL injection on any endpoint; attacker queries payment_settings table
2.1.3. SELECT * FROM payment_settings WHERE processor='Cryptomus'; attacker exfiltrates key
2.2. Exfiltrate Keys from File System
2.2.1. Keys hardcoded in /app/config.php
2.2.2. LFI via ?page=../../config.php endpoint
2.2.3. Path traversal on file download endpoint
2.2.4. Backup files (.env.bak, config.php~) readable in web root
2.3. Keys Exposed in Error Messages / Logs
2.3.1. Payment processor API errors logged with full response (includes key)
2.3.2. Debug mode enabled in production; /debug or phpinfo() exposes env vars
2.3.3. Error page displays exception stack trace with config include paths
2.4. Keys Accessible via Admin Panel (IDOR / Auth Bypass)
2.4.1. Admin panel /admin/payment-settings has no authentication
2.4.2. Normal user escalates to admin via is_admin=1 parameter
2.4.3. Attacker accesses /admin/payment-settings and reads all processor keys
2.5. Direct Withdrawal from Payment Processor
2.5.1. Attacker uses exfiltrated key to make withdrawal request to Cryptomus API
2.5.2. No IP whitelist or rate limit on processor API from application
2.5.3. Funds drained to attacker's wallet in minutes
3. Full Admin Panel Takeover
3.1. Admin Authentication Bypass
3.1.1. Brute force admin password on /admin/login with no rate limit
3.1.2. SQL injection on /admin/login (username' OR '1'='1--)
3.1.3. Default admin credentials not changed (admin/admin, admin/password)
3.1.4. Session fixation: attacker sets cookie before admin logs in
3.2. Privilege Escalation from User to Admin
3.2.1. is_admin flag stored in session/cookie without server-side validation
3.2.2. Attacker modifies cookie (is_admin=1) or session variable
3.2.3. POST /api/update-user?role=admin sets admin role without authorization check
3.2.4. No server-side role validation on protected endpoints
3.3. IDOR on Admin Endpoints
3.3.1. /admin/user-management endpoint has no authentication
3.3.2. /admin/settings/1 returns admin settings even if user is not admin
3.3.3. Attacker iterates through settings IDs and accesses all configuration
3.4. Stored XSS Leading to Admin Session Theft
3.4.1. Stored XSS in user support ticket subject
3.4.2. Admin views ticket list; XSS payload fires in admin session
3.4.3. JavaScript steals admin session cookie and sends to attacker server
3.4.4. Attacker uses admin cookie to access admin panel
3.5. Remote Code Execution via File Upload
3.5.1. Admin upload endpoint accepts .php files disguised as images
3.5.2. File type validation only checks extension, not magic bytes
3.5.3. Attacker uploads shell.php as shell.jpg; renames on server
3.5.4. Attacker accesses /uploads/shell.php?cmd=id and executes commands
3.6. Admin Actions After Takeover
3.6.1. Attacker disables all payment processors to prevent withdrawals
3.6.2. Attacker modifies operator's payout address to attacker wallet
3.6.3. Attacker deletes audit logs to cover tracks
3.6.4. Attacker creates backdoor admin account for persistent access
4. Compromise User Credentials Database (Mass ATO)
4.1. SQL Injection to Dump User Table
4.1.1. SQL injection in any query endpoint (search, filter, login)
4.1.2. Attacker uses UNION-based injection to query users table
4.1.3. SELECT username, email, password FROM users exfiltrated
4.2. Weak Password Hashing
4.2.1. Passwords hashed with MD5 or unsalted SHA1
4.2.2. Attacker uses rainbow table to crack hashes offline
4.2.3. Common passwords recovered in minutes (password, 123456, admin)
4.2.4. Strong passwords would take weeks/months; operator has time to rotate
4.3. Credential Stuffing Attack
4.3.1. Attacker obtains credentials from other breached sites (LinkedIn, etc.)
4.3.2. Attacker tests credentials against mrbeanpanel login
4.3.3. Overlap in users + weak passwords = high success rate (10-30%)
5. Service Disruption / Denial of Service
5.1. Disable Payment Processors
5.1.1. Attacker gains admin access (see branch 3)
5.1.2. Attacker disables all payment processors in /admin/payment-settings
5.1.3. Users cannot top-up balances; new orders cannot be placed
5.2. Mass Delete Orders / Logs
5.2.1. SQL injection enables DELETE FROM orders or DROP TABLE orders
5.2.2. Attacker deletes transaction history to prevent dispute resolution
5.2.3. No backup or recovery; data loss is permanent
5.3. Resource Exhaustion / Database Crash
5.3.1. Attacker crafts expensive SQL query (SELECT * with no WHERE)
5.3.2. Query locks database; legitimate queries timeout
5.3.3. Service degradation or outage until operator kills query

catastrophic_outcomes: Operator loses access to payment processor merchant accounts (keys compromised); attacker withdraws all customer deposits and operator reserves. Financial loss: $50k–$500k+ depending on processor balance.

Mass account takeover (1000+ users) enabled by weak authentication. Attackers drain all visible balances. Users demand refunds; operator's operational credibility collapses. Chargeback liability and regulatory scrutiny (GDPR, MoneyCorp regulations).

Admin panel compromised. Attacker disables payment processors, deletes order history, and installs persistent backdoor. Service unavailable for days. Operator loses entire order pipeline revenue during recovery window.

User credential database (username + password hash) exfiltrated. Weak hashing (MD5, unsalted) enables rapid offline cracking. Credentials sold on dark market. Secondary ATOs occur across multiple platforms using same password.
Audit logs deleted post-breach. Operator cannot prove to regulators or users what happened, when, or to whom. Refund disputes unresolvable. Regulatory penalties and lawsuits follow.
not_in_model: Nation-state adversaries. No geopolitical value in compromising SMM panel; out-of-scope for this threat model.
Physical attacks on infrastructure. Assumes cloud hosting; physical security is cloud provider's responsibility.
Supply-chain attacks on dependencies (PHP, Smarty, nginx). Covered by standard security patching practices; specific CVE-chaining is out of scope.
Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. Infrastructure resilience (WAF, DDoS mitigation) assumed in place; testing is ISP/CDN responsibility.
Side-channel attacks (cache timing, speculative execution). Too low-probability for realistic SMM panel attacker.
Malicious insider intentionally sabotaging (covered under § 3 T4, but excluded from active penetration testing scope; assumes admin honesty).
Accidental misconfiguration (e.g., admin left API key in code comment). Deployment/SDLC issue, not architectural threat.
